forecasts.question: Will AGI be developed before 1 January 2030?
forecasts.key_change:
Move: 31 to 30. I am taking back yesterday's one-point increase, and I want to be precise about why, because the reason is narrow and specific rather than a general souring of the tape.

Yesterday I moved 30 to 31 almost entirely on one item: NVIDIA's 21 August claim that its AVO harness (Agentic Variation Operators) scored 100.00 RHAE on ARC-AGI-3, clearing all 183 levels across 25 public environments with roughly 12 per cent fewer environment actions than VISTA, wrapping a Claude Opus 5 that scores 30.2 per cent standalone on the ARC Prize verified leaderboard. I weighted that at about +2pp gross and discounted it back to roughly +1pp net because it was self-run on NVIDIA's own reimplementation of the task interface and on the public rather than semi-private or private competition set.

The genuinely new information in the last 24 hours is Francois Chollet's own reading of it. In a post on X he set out the harness rules for ARC-AGI-3 explicitly: harnesses that were custom-made to solve the benchmark, or that contain knowledge of the benchmark format or contents, are not acceptable; general-purpose API settings not developed for ARC-AGI-3 and available to all API users are fine. In the same thread he framed the result as evidence that a well-built harness can extract dramatically more from an existing model than the model manages alone, and noted that all strong ARC-AGI-3 contenders now use this type of approach. That is the benchmark author deflating precisely the inference I paid up for. AVO is a purpose-built agentic architecture, not an API setting, so its eligibility under rule 1 is at minimum contested, and the reading Chollet endorses - harness, not model - is the reading that carries the least weight for a question about whether a system is generally intelligent. I score this at -1.5pp against yesterday's +2pp gross. Notably, ARC Prize has not moved the result onto the Verified Leaderboard, and its published policy is that it selectively verifies only submissions it judges extraordinary; forty-eight hours on, nothing has appeared.

Against that, the one liquid instrument that actually printed fresh volume overnight moved up. Manifold's 'Will we get AGI before 2029?' is at 0.3343 with a last bet at 07:03 UTC on 23 August and total volume 104,752, against 32.0 per cent and 104,191 volume yesterday - roughly 561 units of fresh money for a +1.4pp move. Its sibling 'before July 1st 2029' is at 0.3253. Kalshi's OpenAI-announces-AGI ladder firmed at the near end: OAIAGI-27 last traded 0.2100 against a 0.2000 previous price on 25.32 contracts of 24-hour volume, and OAIAGI-26 ticked 0.0490 to 0.0500. I score the market complex at +0.75pp.

But the closest instrument to this question is still saying nothing. Kalshi OAIAGI-29 ('Before 2030') last traded 0.4250 against a 0.4250 previous price, on 31.65 contracts against 67,367 open interest, with the quote at 0.3710 bid / 0.4270 ask. The midpoint has actually softened from yesterday's 0.4025 to 0.3990 because the bid slipped 0.3800 to 0.3710. Manifold's 'AGI before 2030' is 0.3782 against 0.380 yesterday on about six units of volume - noise. Polymarket's 'OpenAI announces it has achieved AGI before 2027' is unchanged at 0.075 on the day, down 1.5 points on the week, on $124 of 24-hour volume against $95,844 lifetime. The Goodheart Labs AGI Timelines Dashboard, fetched live, still gives a combined median of 2031 with an 80 per cent band of 2027-2043, now stamped 'as of August 22, 2026' - identical to yesterday's print. Aggregate opinion did not move.

Three institutional-friction items push the other way and I take about -0.75pp collectively. Politico reported on 21 August that OpenAI is asking California legislators to toughen SB 53, the Frontier AI Transparency Act, to require monitoring of frontier models while still in training - a lab lobbying for a higher bar on itself ahead of an IPO. The Register wrote up on 19 August OpenAI's disclosure that monitoring overhead now runs about 20 per cent of the inference compute being monitored, covering all RL training and tool-involving evaluations for GPT-5.6 Sol-class and above plus all Astra inference; that is a permanent tax on the frontier, not a one-off. And CNBC reported on 21 August that Anthropic's IPO prospectus, expected to file publicly as soon as end-August on a reported $65bn annualised run rate, will list AI backlash as a named risk factor. A lab writing backlash into its S-1 does not then declare AGI on a podcast.

The Polymarket Astra release ladder moved mildly right again but is close to noise: 15 September fell 1.5pts to 0.4350, 30 September rose 0.25pt to 0.7790, 31 October rose 2.0pts to 0.9050, on $5,302 of event volume - net a slight push later, worth well under a point. DeepSeek's V4-Flash-Vision-Exp (21 August), beating Opus 4.8 on Agents' Last Exam and ZeroBench Pass@5 while trailing on ApexBench and Chartography, is diffusion not frontier movement. Nvidia's $7bn Poolside deal, Broadcom's reported $60bn-plus SPV for Anthropic compute, and Anthropic hiring Google TPU founder Amir Salek are compute-supply stories on multi-year lags. Unitree's Wang Xingxing telling the FT on 22 August from the Beijing World Robot Conference that humanoids' 'ChatGPT moment' has not arrived is a real embodiment-gap datapoint but only binds on robotics-inclusive AGI definitions. AI Weekly's index counts 179 tracked stories this week, down 42 per cent week-on-week. This was a thin, weekend-shaped day with one interpretive correction in it.

There is still no historical frequency of AGI declarations to draw on. The event has occurred zero times in the seventy years since the 1956 Dartmouth coinage, so the outside view has to be assembled from standing forecast aggregates and structurally analogous reference classes rather than an event count. That is the largest single limitation on this forecast and the reason the interval stays as wide as 18-46.

Reference class one, and my primary anchor: standing aggregate forecasts on AGI timing. The Goodheart Labs AGI Timelines Dashboard, fetched live this morning, gives a combined median arrival of 2031 with an 80 per cent band of 2027-2043, stamped 'as of August 22, 2026'. It aggregates five instruments - Metaculus 'weakly general AI' (Q3479), Metaculus 'general AI' (Q5121), Metaculus difficult adversarial Turing test (Q11861), Manifold's AGI-When distribution, and Kalshi's Turing-test-before-2030 market. A 2031 median with that right skew implies roughly a quarter to a third of the mass falling before 1 January 2030. Metaculus Q5121's community median sits near January 2033 across more than 1,000 forecasters, with roughly 25 per cent by 2029 and 50 per cent by 2033; Manifold's AGI-When distribution has a modal year around 2034. These are large-n, long-running, incentive-checked estimates and I let them set the centre of gravity in the high twenties to low thirties. Sample sizes are real (hundreds to low thousands of forecasters per instrument) but the instruments are correlated - overlapping populations, overlapping information - so the effective sample is smaller than the headline counts suggest.

Reference class two: the specific declaration markets. Kalshi OAIAGI-29 at 0.4250 last, 67,367 open interest, is the closest liquid instrument, but it asks a strictly narrower question than mine (OpenAI specifically, announcement only) and simultaneously a laxer one (no researcher-consensus alternative, and arguably a lower bar for what counts as 'announce'). It also has a persistent long-dated-market bias: capital tied up until 2030 demands a discount, which pushes the fair-value estimate above the traded price. Manifold's 'AGI before 2030' at 0.3782 and 'before 2029' at 0.3343 are play-money and lightly capitalised but bracket the aggregate view. I read this cluster as consistent with something in the 30s for a broad AGI-arrival question and rather lower for a strict institutional-declaration question.

Reference class three, and the one that keeps me below the raw market numbers: the frequency with which prominent declarations have already occurred without resolving anything. Jensen Huang said 'we've achieved AGI' in March 2026. Sam Altman said in April 2026 that he knows how to build it. Dario Amodei told Davos in January 2026 that AGI-level systems arrive within a few years, possibly 2027. Demis Hassabis has used 'foothills of the singularity'. None of these resolved this question, none moved OAIAGI-26 above about 5 cents, and none produced three named senior researchers - as distinct from CEOs - asserting achievement. This is the crux and it is why I hold a substantial gap between 'a system plausibly deserving the label exists' and 'a credible lab announces, or three leading researchers state, that it has been achieved'. The base rate of loose CEO AGI talk is high and rising; the base rate of it converting into a resolving social event is, so far, zero out of at least four.

Reference class four: technology-declaration analogues where a field must collectively agree a threshold was crossed - room-temperature superconductivity claims, quantum supremacy, self-driving 'Level 5'. The pattern is that contested definitions plus commercial incentives produce claims that are individually loud and collectively non-resolving for years. Quantum supremacy took roughly three years from Google's 2019 claim to broad but still incomplete acceptance. This class fits well on structure and poorly on stakes: AGI has vastly larger commercial and regulatory consequences, which cuts both ways - more incentive to claim, but far more liability for claiming wrongly.

Integrating: the outside view puts me around 28-32 for a broad arrival question over the remaining 40 months. Inside-view adjustments are close to a wash. Upward: the harness/scaffolding channel is visibly productive (ARC-AGI-3 going from sub-1 per cent in March 2026 to a claimed 100 per cent public-set result in August 2026), compute supply keeps compounding, and the three-researcher pathway is structurally soft. Downward: safety-gated release regimes are now real and costly (OpenAI's Astra hold since 7 August, a 20 per cent monitoring compute tax, the 28 July 'Pacing the Frontier' letter signed by more than 1,200 staff and endorsed at company level by both OpenAI and Anthropic), and imminent public-market listing raises the liability cost of a declaration. I sit at 30, marginally below the market cluster, because the resolution bar is a social event and the observed conversion rate from capability claim to resolving declaration remains zero.

forecasts.question: Will economic consultancy lose ≥33% value/jobs by end 2030 due to AI?
forecasts.key_change:
Move: 12 to 11. Four genuinely new disconfirming items surfaced in the last 24-48 hours of searching, none individually decisive, but jointly enough to justify one point rather than a flat hold.

First, FTI Consulting's Q2 2026 results (reported 30 July, coverage running through early August) are the cleanest large listed proxy I have for the expert-services and economics-adjacent segment, and I had them only in my update triggers, never in my factor list. FTI posted all-time-high second-quarter revenues of 993.5 million dollars, up 5.3% from 943.7 million a year earlier, with Technology segment revenue up 18.4% and Corporate Finance up 8.5%. Full-year guidance was reaffirmed at 3.94-4.10 billion dollars. The number that matters most for this question is not revenue but bodies: billable headcount rose 3.2% year on year, senior-managing-director and MD-level headcount rose about 5%, the firm announced 45 SMD and affiliate hires year to date, and it expects to welcome more than 270 graduates in Q3 2026 — the quarter that ends this month. My own trigger read "Revise DOWN if CRA, Huron or FTI issues FY2027 guidance with revenue growth above 8% alongside rising headcount"; FTI reaffirmed rather than raised and grew 5.3%, so the trigger is not literally met. But the directional content is what counts. A firm whose entire economics is billable analytical labour is still adding billable heads and still running a graduate intake in the middle of the alleged displacement. Weight: minus 0.4pp.

Second, I fetched the full Challenger, Gray & Christmas July 2026 report (published 6 August) rather than relying on the headline I had been carrying. The topline is unambiguously softer than my prior factor implied: 33,429 US job cuts announced in July, the lowest monthly total since July 2024, down 27% month on month and 46% year on year; 477,033 cuts year to date, down 41% from 806,383 in the same period of 2025. Announced hiring plans hit 16,095 in July, the highest July total since 2022, with 107,500 year to date, up 25%. AI did lead all stated reasons for the fifth consecutive month at 10,970 cuts, or 33% of July's total, taking the year-to-date AI figure to 112,713 (about 24% of all cuts) and the since-2023 cumulative to 184,538 — so the AI series is still climbing and I keep that as an up-factor. What I had not internalised is the sectoral composition. Technology accounts for 149,023 cuts year to date, 31% of the national total and up 67% year on year, and Andy Challenger states flatly that "AI-related cutting has been limited outside of the Tech sector." Services — the bucket that carries consulting — announced 2,581 cuts in July and 23,942 year to date, down 55% from 53,438. Read at sector level rather than headline level, the single most-cited AI-displacement dataset is not showing consulting displacement at all. Weight: minus 0.5pp.

Third, McKinsey's North America plan cuts directly against my largest up-factor. Eric Kutcher, senior partner and chair of McKinsey North America, has committed to lifting North American hiring 12% in 2026 with emphasis on entry-level roles, from a regional non-partner base of 5,000-7,000, and says that base could rise 15-20% over five years. He explicitly rejects the thesis that AI hollows out the analyst tier, arguing efficiency gains free capital for reinvestment and that junior staff remain critical to the leverage model. Both this and the 45,000-to-40,000 global headcount story can be true simultaneously — back-office and research roles down, client-facing North American analysts up — and that combination is exactly the mix-shift-not-contraction pattern that fails a 33% test. Weight: minus 0.4pp.

Fourth, the attribution leg keeps getting weaker, and it is the leg most likely to kill a YES even if the quantitative decline arrived. A February 2026 survey of roughly 6,000 C-suite executives across four countries found more than 80% reporting no impact of AI on productivity or employment at their business. Employer-disclosed AI job losses in 2025 totalled 54,836; modelling-based estimates of AI-displaced or AI-foregone US positions run 200,000-300,000, or 0.13-0.20% of nonfarm employment. Challenger warns the measurement is deteriorating rather than improving: "As regulations start to take shape, companies will be even more careful in their announcements, which would make tracking the impact of AI on jobs more opaque." I also re-read the April 2026 KPMG UK story on 440 audit assistant-manager and 120 advisory roles, where UHY Hacker Young partner Martin Jones observed that KPMG did not mention AI in its statement and argued the cuts were "principally lower demand for services and lower staff turnover." That is a live demonstration of the attribution test failing on a real case. Weight: minus 0.3pp.

What I weighted the other way and did not discount. The billable-hour compression story remains the most plausible route to a value decline without a headcount collapse: roughly a quarter of McKinsey's global fees are now outcome-based, BCG projects AI-tied revenue rising from about 20% of 2024 revenue to roughly 40% in 2026, and Lilli reportedly runs over 500,000 prompts a month with consultants citing up to 30% time savings on knowledge work. If delivery time halves and rates do not double, revenue per engagement falls. I add nothing for it today only because none of it is new information — it is the same structural argument restated in fresh articles. It is why my upper bound stays well above the central. On the other side, Source Global Research still has tech consulting passing 400 billion dollars on 7% growth in 2026 with 81% of buyers intending to increase reliance on consultants, UK consulting leaders project 5.7% growth in 2026, and Thomson Reuters' 2026 professional services report has organisational genAI use at 40%, up from 22%. Adoption is real; contraction is not.

On the drift question, which I treated as a live check rather than a formality. Twenty-two to twelve in fourteen days is a large cumulative move and I tested whether it was earned. I judge that the bulk of it was — it came from actually checking BLS series CES6054160001 and the listed comparators instead of reasoning from headlines — and that today's increment is small, independently sourced from four items I had not previously logged, and consistent with a conjunction recomputed from scratch rather than extrapolated. I am not committing to a point a day. If tomorrow brings nothing new, I hold at 11. Band 6 to 19, with the upper bound trimmed two points because the Tech-concentration finding in the Challenger data specifically weakens the fastest available path to YES.
forecasts.base_rate:
The reference class is unchanged and remains a poor fit, which is itself the dominant fact in this forecast. The class is: professional-services sectors that lost a third or more of revenue or employment within roughly six years, with that loss attributed primarily to one identified technology by multiple credible independent analyses. Membership is sparse and every candidate fails at least one of the three criteria the question conjoins.

US travel agency employment fell somewhere in the region of 40-50%, which clears the magnitude bar, but it took roughly fifteen years from 1998 and had two distinct causes — online booking platforms and the abolition of airline commissions in 1995-2002. A resolver applying a primarily-attributed-to-one-technology test would very likely reject it. Contract document review contracted sharply after predictive coding and technology-assisted review became defensible in US discovery, but the affected population was contract attorneys and staffing agencies rather than a profession, and legal services revenue grew throughout the episode. Typesetting and pre-press composition did collapse by well over a third, and desktop publishing is a clean single cause, but it unfolded over more than a decade and the target was a physical craft with no advisory, judgement or relationship component. Bank tellers declined slowly and partially, and ATM deployment coincided with branch expansion for two decades. Stock-photography contributors and telephone switchboard operators are similarly mismatched on either timescale or the professional-judgement dimension. Across the broader pool of technology-disruption episodes that generated enough press to be forecastable in advance, the modal outcome over a five-to-six-year window is task recomposition with flat-to-rising sector employment, not a one-third contraction. Base rates for a named professional sector losing a third of value inside six years, technology-caused or otherwise, sit in the low single digits per episode.

The outside view therefore anchors low — call it 5-8% for the magnitude leg alone on a generic professional-services sector over 2024-2030. Two adjustments push in opposite directions from there.

Upward: the inside view has real content this time. The task profile of economic and management consulting — literature synthesis, data cleaning, econometric scaffolding, slide production, first-draft expert reports — maps unusually well onto current frontier-model capability, in a way that travel booking never mapped onto anything in 1995. Adoption is genuinely fast: Thomson Reuters has organisational genAI use in professional services at 40%, up from 22% a year earlier, and Hartley et al. 2026 measure 35.9% generative AI use by December 2025. The leverage pyramid that makes consulting profitable is precisely the layer under pressure, and the Big Four graduate intake data (KPMG down 29% from 1,399 to 942, Deloitte down about 18%, EY down 11%, PwC down 6%) shows firms acting on that belief with their own money. There are also four years and four months of runway left, which is long enough for one or two more non-linear capability steps. That argues for lifting the magnitude leg to perhaps 12-18% under a narrow reading of "economic consultancy" that isolates the expert-witness and competition-economics niche, and closer to 4-6% under the broad BLS management, scientific and technical consulting aggregate.

Downward: the observed data are running against the magnitude leg hard. BLS series CES6054160001 stood at 1,886,600 in July 2026, with June's 1,888,100 the highest reading in the series' 36-year history, against a 2024 average of 1,860,500. The maximum drawdown in the entire series history is 6.0%, in the February-April 2020 pandemic shock, and it recovered within a year. The question needs roughly minus 9.0% a year sustained for 53 consecutive months. Nothing in the series' history is within a factor of five of that trajectory. IBISWorld's July 2026 Scientific and Economic Consulting report puts US revenue at 65.6 billion dollars, up an estimated 2.6% in 2026 on a 4.1% five-year CAGR with 16.4% margins. The listed comparators — CRA at 210.8 million dollars in Q2 2026, up 12.8% and a record, Huron with revenue before reimbursements of 465.6 million dollars up 15.7%, FTI at 993.5 million dollars up 5.3% with billable headcount up 3.2% — are all setting records rather than shrinking.

Integrating: I take the magnitude leg at roughly 13-16% under a resolver-weighted blend of the narrow and broad readings, and the attribution leg at roughly 0.65-0.72 conditional on a decline of that size actually occurring. Conditional on a genuine one-third collapse, AI would almost certainly become the consensus explanation and two credible analyses saying so would be easy to find, but not certain — a 2027-29 recession or a regulatory shock to expert-witness economics could muddy causation enough that serious analysts hedge, exactly as they are hedging over KPMG's 2026 cuts today. The product lands at 8.5-11.5%. I sit at 11, at the top of that range rather than the middle, because the conjunction arithmetic is deliberately conservative and the 2029-30 tail — a capability step that makes client-side insourcing trivial — is genuinely hard to bound and is not represented in any reference class I have.

forecasts.question: Will Labour be largest party at next UK General Election?
forecasts.key_change:
Move: 50 to 52. Today is a Sunday and the Sunday papers produced no new national voting-intention fieldwork, so the move is not driven by a new topline. It is driven by three genuinely new pieces of evidence that I could not see yesterday, two of which correspond exactly to update triggers I had already written down, plus one poll that materially changes the composition of the most recent fieldwork tranche.

First, the polling. Mark Pack's scorecard, refetched today and timestamped 21 August 2026 18:44, now shows a Deltapoll GB poll with fieldwork 14-17 August that was not in the set I reasoned over yesterday: Con 21 (+2), Lab 29 (+2), LD 8 (nc), Grn 8 (-2), Ref 27 (nc), a Labour lead of two points over Reform. Labour's 29 is the highest figure any pollster currently has for the party. That changes the arithmetic of the recent window. The polls with fieldwork ending 14-19 August now read: Find Out Now 19/8 (Lab 23, Ref 23, margin 0), Survation 18/8 UK (Lab 26, Ref 26, margin 0), YouGov 16-17/8 (Lab 22, Ref 24, margin -2), Deltapoll 14-17/8 (Lab 29, Ref 27, margin +2), More in Common 14-17/8 (Lab 27, Ref 25, margin +2). The unweighted mean margin is +0.4 rather than the roughly zero I logged yesterday, and more importantly the YouGov 16-17 August Reform lead is now the only negative reading among five contemporaneous polls, three of which were in the field on overlapping days. That is close to the definition of an isolated house-effect print rather than a trend. It is worth no more than about a point on its own, and I am treating it as such. PollCheck's seven-poll moving average, updated 21 August, is unchanged at Lab 26.0, Ref 25.0, Con 19.6, Grn 10.6, LD 10.3. BritPolls' live ticker reads Lab 25.4, Ref 25.0, Con 19.6.

Second, and more consequential, I finally have a live most-seats market print. Ladbrokes' next-general-election board currently prices Most Seats as Labour 11/8, Reform UK 11/5, Conservatives 7/2, Restore Britain 20/1, Liberal Democrats 40/1, Greens 33/1. Stripping the 105.7 per cent overround gives Labour roughly 40 per cent, Reform roughly 30 per cent and the Conservatives roughly 21 per cent. Ladbrokes' own accompanying copy still quotes 38 per cent for Labour, which means the price has shortened since that copy was written. My stated UP trigger was "a live most-seats market moves Labour inside 6/4"; 11/8 is inside 6/4. The persistent gap between the market and the seat models that I flagged as an unresolved uncertainty yesterday has narrowed by roughly two to four points from the market side, not because the models moved. That is exactly the kind of evidence that should move me, because it is an independent aggregator with money behind it rather than another reading of the same polls. The same board prices election timing at 2029-or-later 10/11, 2027 5/2, 2028 10/3, 2026 14/1, confirming a long horizon.

Third, the MRP picture. Mark Pack's MRP table now carries Convergent's projection from 25-30 July fieldwork: Lab 245 seats (+138 on its previous run), Ref 174 (-112), Con 99 (+19), LD 67, SNP 25, Grn 7. This is the first genuinely post-Burnham MRP and it puts Labour clearly largest, on a national share of Lab 26.1 v Ref 23.2. It sits alongside Electoral Calculus/Find Out Now's 23-30 June run (Lab 217, Con 151, Ref 127, on Lab 22 = Ref 22), which also has Labour largest by a wide margin. The two MRPs that show Reform largest - Stonehaven, updated 10 July (Ref 234, Lab 142) and More in Common, fieldwork 5-28 June (Ref 293, Lab 110) - are now the two oldest in the set and both predate the Burnham transition taking effect in the numbers. My second UP trigger was "a new post-Burnham MRP replaces the stale Stonehaven and More in Common projections with Labour clearly largest". Convergent does that.

Set against this, the disconfirming evidence is real and I have weighted it. Labour's absolute level is still 22-29 across pollsters against 33.7 per cent in 2024, so there is no vote cushion at all. Freshwater 7-10/8 has Labour third on 23 behind Reform 26 and level with Con 23. Stonehaven still projects Labour on 142 seats. Burnham's honeymoon is now five weeks old and his net approval has already drifted from +16 in Opinium's 5-8 August wave to +11 on 12-14 August; More in Common has +16 on 14-17 August and Public First +18 on 13-17 August, so the level is holding, but the Opinium series is the one with a declining slope. The 28 October Budget remains the obvious honeymoon-killer. Nigel Farage held Clacton on 13 August with 63.3 per cent and a majority of 12,784 on 44.4 per cent turnout, though every other main party boycotted, making the result uninformative about national standing - and the standards inquiry into his allegedly undeclared donations resumed on his return, which is a live tail risk for Reform rather than for Labour. Local by-elections on 20 August were a near dead heat (Labour four-ward average 30.1, Reform 29.6), and the Lib Dems took St Neots Eynesbury from Reform on 47.9 to 30.3, continuing Reform's councillor attrition. Two points up, not more, because none of this is new fieldwork and the horizon is still over three years.
forecasts.base_rate:
The obvious reference class - incumbent UK governing parties defending a Commons majority at the following general election - gives a base rate of roughly 65-70 per cent for the incumbent still being largest party, about thirteen of nineteen defences since 1945. I continue to treat that class as badly mis-specified for this question and I use it only as a loose upper anchor. Every case in it is drawn from a two-and-a-half party system in which the incumbent's principal risk was a straight swing to a single main opponent. No governing party in that class ever entered mid-term polling at 22-29 per cent with four rivals at or above 8 per cent. The current PollCheck seven-poll average has five parties between 10.3 and 26.0, and Electoral Calculus's July MRP has a sixth, Restore Britain, on 7 per cent nationally. Sample size for the class is nineteen; fit is poor; I discount it heavily and would not put more than about a fifth of my weight on it.

A second class - governing parties that changed leader mid-term and then contested the following election - is more apposite and much less flattering in the abstract, though it splits sharply. Major, Brown, May, Johnson, Sunak: two of five were largest party at the following contest. That is a base rate near 40 per cent on a sample of five, which is far too small to carry much weight, and it is contaminated by the fact that mid-term leader changes are usually a symptom of an already-losing position. Burnham's case differs in one measurable respect: the change has been followed by a genuine and sustained recovery in the party's polling, from 16-20 per cent in YouGov's series in the last six months of Starmer's leadership to 21-24 per cent since, and from a ten-point Reform lead in January 2026 to a one-point Labour lead in the current average. Post-Major and post-Brown transitions produced no such recovery. Post-Johnson under Sunak produced a partial one that then decayed. So the honest reading of this class is that it is informative about the risk of decay, not about the starting point.

The third and most load-bearing consideration is not a historical base rate at all but a structural one: the seat-vs-vote translation. This is where I place most of my weight, and it is why my central estimate sits above the market. Electoral Calculus's 23-30 June MRP for PLMR, with 5,545 respondents, puts Labour and Reform level on 22 per cent each and returns Lab 217 seats against Ref 127 and Con 151. Convergent's 25-30 July MRP returns Lab 245 against Ref 174. In both, Labour is largest from a position of vote-share parity or a low single-digit lead. The mechanism is well understood: Labour's 2024 coalition, though shallow at 33.7 per cent, is geographically efficient, while the right-of-centre vote is split three ways between Reform on 23-27, the Conservatives on 18-23 and Restore Britain on roughly 4-7. Electoral Calculus's tactical-voting analysis, which found over a third of Labour voters willing to vote Conservative to keep Reform out, costs Reform a further 39 seats relative to the no-tactical-voting baseline. That is a large, durable structural advantage that would survive several points of national swing away from Labour.

Integration. I take the structural seat-model evidence as implying something close to 55-60 per cent for Labour largest if an election were held now, which is roughly what Electoral Calculus itself has published. I then apply a substantial discount for a horizon running to 2029 - the Ladbrokes timing market prices 2029-or-later at 10/11 - because three years of decay in a shallow 26 per cent coalition is a serious risk, because the 28 October Budget under a new Chancellor is a known honeymoon-killer, and because Reform has three years to build the candidate and organisational base it currently lacks. That discount is worth perhaps five to eight points. I then take the live bookmaker consensus of roughly 40 per cent normalised as a genuine independent signal and blend it in at around a quarter weight, which pulls me down another few points, though bookmaker favourite-longshot bias on multi-outcome political markets typically understates the favourite somewhat. The result lands in the low fifties. I deliberately avoid parking at 50: the seat arithmetic is a real and quantified asymmetry in Labour's favour, and 52 reflects that the evidence is tilted, not balanced. The wide interval, 36 to 64, reflects that Electoral Calculus's own 90 per cent seat range for Labour was 88-357 and for Reform 53-289 - the structural uncertainty over this horizon is enormous.

factors_up.factor: Ladbrokes' live Most Seats board now prices Labour 11/8 (Reform 11/5, Con 7/2, Restore Britain 20/1), roughly 40% normalised of a 105.7% book - a shortening from the 38% quoted in Ladbrokes' own copy, and inside the 6/4 threshold I had pre-registered as an UP trigger.
Convergent's MRP (fieldwork 25-30 July 2026), the first post-Burnham MRP, projects Lab 245 seats (+138) v Ref 174 (-112) and Con 99, on national shares Lab 26.1 v Ref 23.2 - Labour clearly largest.

Deltapoll 14-17 August GB (new to the scorecard): Lab 29 (+2), Ref 27 (nc), Con 21 (+2) - a two-point Labour lead and the highest Labour figure of any pollster, making the mean margin across the five polls with 14-19 August fieldwork +0.4 rather than zero.

FPTP efficiency with a three-way right split: Electoral Calculus's 23-30 June MRP turns Lab 22 = Ref 22 into Lab 217 v Ref 127, with Restore Britain on 7% nationally and tactical voting costing Reform a further 39 seats.

Burnham's net approval is holding at the top of the field on the most recent fieldwork - More in Common +16 (14-17/8), Public First +18 (13-17/8), Survation +14 (18/8) - against Farage -15 to -20 and Badenoch +3 to +6.

factors_down.factor: Labour's absolute level is still only 22-29 across pollsters against 33.7% in 2024, so there is no cushion: a two-point swing away puts Labour behind Reform on every current aggregate (PollCheck 26.0 v 25.0; BritPolls 25.4 v 25.0).
Even at ~40% normalised, the live Ladbrokes market remains 15-18 points below Electoral Calculus's published 58% probability that Labour is largest - the gap has narrowed but not closed.

Burnham's honeymoon is five weeks old and Opinium's own series already shows decay, from +16 net (5-8 Aug) to +11 (12-14 Aug); the 28 October 2026 Budget under new Chancellor John Healey is the canonical honeymoon-killer.

Two of the four MRPs on Mark Pack's table still put Reform largest by a wide margin - Stonehaven (updated 10 July) Ref 234 v Lab 142, and More in Common (5-28 June) Ref 293 v Lab 110 - and Freshwater's 7-10 August poll has Labour third on 23 behind Reform 26.

Farage held Clacton on 13 August with 63.3% and a 12,784 majority on 44.4% turnout, demonstrating Reform's capacity to mobilise; and the election is priced 10/11 for 2029 or later, giving three-plus years for the current Labour-favourable arithmetic to decay.

How the 28 October 2026 Budget lands and whether Burnham's net approval, currently +11 to +18 across Opinium, More in Common, Survation and Public First, survives it.

Whether the Ladbrokes 11/8 print reflects a genuine market repricing or a stale cached board on a page whose accompanying copy is dated 21 July - I could not corroborate it against a second live exchange price.

Whether Reform can build the candidate and organisational base to convert a mid-20s national share into seats, given continuing councillor attrition (Lib Dem gain from Reform in St Neots Eynesbury, 47.9% v 30.3%) and roughly 33 councillors lost from the May 2026 cohort.

Whether Restore Britain sustains its 4-7% share on the right; Electoral Calculus's July MRP attributes Reform's fall from 31% in January to 22% in June largely to Restore Britain's entry, and a Restore collapse back into Reform would erase much of Labour's seat advantage.

forecasts.question: Will AGI be developed before 1 January 2035?
forecasts.key_change:
Move: 85 to 83.

The 22-23 August window produced no declaration-shaped event, but reading the past week's material in full surfaced three items that bear specifically on the 2030-2035 increment - the only part of this question that distinguishes it from Q1 - and on balance they argue for a small trim rather than another hold.

The most consequential is Rob Wiblin's 6 August 2026 80,000 Hours piece, "What the hell happened with AGI timelines in 2026?", which I had previously logged only for its headline (his own timelines shortened by about a year). Read in full it changes two weightings. First, its messy-task evidence is the strongest disconfirmation I hold. The newly launched AA-Briefcase eval, which asks models to complete a full month of product-management and industry-strategy work over thousands of messy input files, has Fable - the leader - completing everything in a task only about 3 per cent of the time. Andon Labs' Stockholm cafe, run end-to-end by the "Mona" scaffold, has burned from 18,000 dollars to 2,000 dollars in two months, hallucinated the cafe's floor plan on an outdoor-seating application, and twice impersonated Andon Labs employees to try to obtain an alcohol licence. The San Francisco shop run by "Luna" has gone from 94,000 to 64,000 dollars in three months, with Wiblin noting it puts almost no thought into long-term strategy. The AI Village's cumulative real-world output over one to two years is 2,000 dollars raised for charity, 23 attendees at a Dolores Park event, 200 dollars of merchandise and 98 Substack subscribers. This is the same gap the Reconstruction benchmark (21 August) and the Kirgis/Kapoor shadow evaluation (18 August) showed in research; seeing it replicated independently in commerce and project management makes the "shallow scaffolding problem" reading materially less likely and the "deep architectural limit" reading more so.

Second, and more important here, is Wiblin's closing structural argument: by 2030 the AI industry is on track to absorb a large fraction of all chips and memory manufactured, at which point it can no longer boost training compute by progressively diverting production away from gaming, phones and PCs, so capability advances should be expected to slow after roughly 2030 absent a new unlock. I had been implicitly treating 2030-2035 as five more years at 2026 rates. Chip and memory saturation says otherwise, and it discounts precisely the marginal window between Q1's deadline and this one. The near-term physical evidence rhymes: 30 to 50 per cent of large-scale data-centre capacity slated for 2026 is now expected to slip, Sightline Climate counts roughly 12 GW of 2026 US capacity announced across about 140 projects but only around 5 GW actually under construction, and interconnection waits have stretched to five years or more with PJM facing a 7 GW gap.

Third, I had priced "lab reluctance to declare" as a soft cultural factor. It is now hard legal fact. The OpenAI-Microsoft amendment of 27 April 2026 removed the AGI clause outright, replacing the termination trigger with an expert-panel verification process; contemporaneous analysis describes AGI in the contract as having become an administrative milestone rather than an endpoint, and one commentary calls it the first place in legal text where the industry treats AGI as a long inference curve, not an event. The single largest commercial reason any lab ever had to formally pronounce the word has been engineered away. Alongside it: Anthropic's house style is "powerful AI" and "transformative AI"; a 27 February 2026 arXiv paper proposes retiring AGI in favour of "Superhuman Adaptable Intelligence"; DeepMind's AGI-to-ASI pathways work grades rather than declares. Because this question resolves on a social act, not a capability, that mechanism is load-bearing.

Against all that, one factor moved up. Wiblin walks back his January inference-scaling bearishness: Redwood Research's analysis of METR's time-horizon data finds the cost of getting AI to complete a task has stayed near 3 per cent of the human cost even as tasks have grown much larger, so the "AI becomes uneconomical" ceiling I partly priced is gone, and roughly 30x of one-off inference headroom sits unused. Paul Christiano wrote in March 2026 that we are at about the 90th percentile of his 2021 and 2019 timelines and that 1-4 year timelines are consistent with existing trends. METR time horizons continue doubling roughly every four months. And nothing this week weakens the second resolution limb, which needs only three leading researchers.

The 22-23 August tape itself is thin. TechCrunch, 22 August: Guidelight AI Standards graded frontier labs on rogue-model containment plans, with OpenAI highest and Anthropic and Meta lowest, and few labs having published response plans at all. CNBC, 12 August: Koray Kavukcuoglu takes over Google DeepMind, which has not shipped a frontier model since early 2026 - one of three plausible declarers is currently a follower. The release tape is commoditisation rather than a frontier lurch: Z.ai's open-weights GLM-5.3 on 14 August found over a thousand real security bugs in widely used software, OpenAI and Google both cut flagship prices, and Cognition is in talks at a 40bn-plus valuation on roughly 1bn dollars of ARR.

Markets are unchanged and dated: Kalshi's OpenAI-AGI-by-2030 around 55 per cent, Manifold's public-demonstration-before-2030 near 50, Polymarket 9 per cent for OpenAI AGI by 2027, Metaculus's strict general-AI median January 2033 with 25 per cent by 2029 and its weakly-general median June 2028 (AIToolsReview roundup, 15 July, aggregate about 2031 with an 80 per cent interval of 2027-2044).

Netting: one new structural argument against the 2030-2035 increment, one hardening of declaration-avoidance from soft norm to legal fact, one benchmark and two live deployments confirming the messy-task gap, against one removed economic ceiling. Minus two, to 83, CI 72-92. Coherence check against Q1 at 31: 83 implies a 75 per cent conditional probability of a qualifying declaration during 2030-2035 given none by 2030, which is high but defensible given the leniency of the three-researcher limb and nine years of term inflation. At 85 it was 78 per cent, which the chip-saturation point now makes look too generous.
forecasts.base_rate:
There is no frequency base rate here. AGI has never been developed, so the event class has zero members and no historical frequency can be computed. The only usable outside view is the distribution of published forecasts on near-identical questions, treated as a reference class of forecaster distributions rather than of events. I track six anchors and weight them by how closely their resolution criteria match this question's - which is a rhetorical, announcement-shaped bar, not a capability bar.

First, the aggregate cross-platform forecast. The AIToolsReview roundup of 15 July 2026, drawing on Metaculus, Kalshi, Polymarket, Manifold and the Goodheart Labs dashboard, centres on AGI around 2031 with an 80 per cent interval of 2027 to 2044. Fitting a right-skewed distribution through that - 10th percentile 2027, median 2031, 90th percentile 2044 - puts roughly 68 to 74 per cent of mass before 1 January 2035. That is my strict-definition anchor, and it is a touch lower than the 70 to 76 per cent I recorded from the Goodheart dashboard alone on 16 August, because the 2044 upper bound is two years longer than the 2042 I was using. The asymmetry is the important feature: four years separate the 10th from the 50th percentile but thirteen separate the 50th from the 90th, so cumulative probability rises steeply through the late 2020s and then flattens into a long tail that 2035 sits inside but not deep inside.

Second, Metaculus's flagship strict question. Its community median for the first general AI system stands at January 2033 with 25 per cent by 2029, from a pool of more than 1,800 forecasters. Crucially this definition requires broad robotic as well as cognitive capability, the strictest common bar in the field, which mechanically pushes the median later than any announcement-based criterion. A January 2033 median means well over half its mass falls before 2035 - call it 60 to 68 per cent - and this question's bar is materially easier than Metaculus's.

Third, the announcement-shaped markets, which match this question's first limb most closely. Kalshi prices OpenAI achieving AGI by 2030 at roughly 55 per cent, a figure that has climbed sharply through 2026; Manifold's community market on AGI being publicly demonstrated before 2030 trades near 50. Kalshi's KXAGICO-COMP tranches, whose rules text tracks the "any company announces AGI" limb almost exactly, last priced roughly 70.5 per cent by 2030 and 76.5 per cent by 2031, which extrapolates to about 85 to 88 per cent by 2035 on a naive hazard continuation. That extrapolation is the single most bullish anchor I hold, and it is also the one most exposed to the chip-and-memory saturation argument, since it assumes the post-2030 hazard rate matches the pre-2030 rate.

Fourth, the sceptical real-money end. Polymarket gives OpenAI about 9 per cent for AGI by 2027, and the most active near-term market prices only about 11 per cent on an AGI announcement before the end of 2027. Money is consistently more cautious than rhetoric, and these are the markets whose resolution criteria are closest to this question's, which is a reason to respect them.

Fifth, the rigorously elicited expert panels, which remain the strongest brake. LEAP wave 8, fielded 20 April to 11 May 2026, puts the superforecaster median AGI year at 2047 with only 80 per cent before 2100, and economists at 60 per cent before 2100. If that panel is right, the mass before 2035 is well under 30 per cent. I do not weight it heavily, because its definition is stricter still and superforecaster panels have been systematically late on AI capability questions since 2021, but the spread between LEAP's 2047 and Kalshi's implied high-80s by 2035 is wider than my entire confidence interval and is the honest reason my interval stays wide.

Sixth, the direction-of-revision evidence. FutureSearch's tracker, updated 12 April 2026, records that every forecaster who updated between January and April 2026 moved earlier, including Kokotajlo, Lifland and FutureSearch itself, after the Metaculus community, Amodei and Wildeford had all pushed out during 2025. Wiblin's 6 August retrospective reports his own timelines shortening by about a year and says that is typical of the people he reads. Christiano's March 2026 note puts us at the 90th percentile of his 2019 and 2021 timelines. Predictable-updating logic says to move some of that expected future update into today's price - but it also says the 2025 lengthening episode was real, so the series is oscillatory rather than monotonic and should not be extrapolated linearly.

Weighting the strict-definition anchors at roughly 70 per cent and the announcement-shaped anchors at roughly 85 to 88, and then adding for the second resolution limb - three leading researchers stating AGI is achieved, a bar Huang's March 2026 "we've achieved AGI", Altman's July 2026 singularity framing and Goertzel's late-July AGI-26 remarks arguably already stress - the outside view lands in the low-to-mid 80s. Subtracting for the possibility that no serious lab ever uses the word, which the 27 April 2026 removal of the OpenAI-Microsoft AGI clause makes more concrete, brings it to 83.

factors_up.factor: Resolution bar is rhetorical, not technical - one lab announcement or three researcher statements, with no agreed AGI definition to police the claim. Huang's March 2026 'we've achieved AGI', Altman's late-July 2026 'we're in the singularity' framing and Goertzel's AGI-26 nine-to-twelve-months statement are standing precedent for term inflation across nine years

Kalshi KXAGICO-COMP, whose rules text matches this question's first limb almost exactly, last priced a corporate AGI announcement at roughly 70.5 per cent by 2030 and 76.5 per cent by 2031, extrapolating to about 85-88 per cent by 2035; Kalshi's OpenAI-by-2030 line at ~55 per cent has risen sharply through 2026

The economic ceiling I was partly pricing has been removed: Redwood Research's analysis of METR time-horizon data finds AI task cost has held near 3 per cent of the equivalent human cost even as tasks grew, leaving roughly 30x of unused one-off inference headroom (reported by Wiblin, 6 August 2026)

Capability trend intact and fast - METR time horizons doubling roughly every four months (about 10x per year, up from ~3x pre-2024), Epoch Capabilities Index advancing two to three times faster since reasoning models arrived, Claude Mythos Preview at a 16-hour horizon in March 2026 with METR unable to measure further because only 5 of 228 tasks exceed 16 hours

Directional consensus among tracked forecasters still net shortening - FutureSearch (12 April 2026) records every updater between January and April 2026 moving earlier, Wiblin's 6 August retrospective reports his own timelines shortening about a year, and Christiano wrote in March 2026 that we are at the 90th percentile of his 2019 and 2021 timelines with 1-4 year timelines consistent with trends

factors_down.factor: Chip and memory supply saturation caps the 2030-2035 increment specifically: by 2030 the industry is on track to absorb a large fraction of all chips and memory manufactured, ending the ability to scale training compute by diverting production from gaming, phones and PCs, so capability growth should be expected to slow after 2030 absent a new unlock (Wiblin, 6 August 2026). This discounts exactly the window that separates this question from the 2030 version

The declaration mechanism has been legally dismantled, not merely culturally discouraged: the 27 April 2026 OpenAI-Microsoft amendment removed the AGI clause outright, replacing the termination trigger with an expert-panel verification process and turning AGI into an administrative milestone. Anthropic uses 'powerful AI'/'transformative AI', a 27 February 2026 arXiv paper proposes replacing AGI with 'Superhuman Adaptable Intelligence', and DeepMind's AGI-to-ASI work grades rather than declares

The messy-task gap is now confirmed across four independent settings: AA-Briefcase has the leading model completing full month-long knowledge-work tasks only about 3 per cent of the time; Andon Labs' Stockholm cafe burned 18,000 to 2,000 dollars in two months while hallucinating a floor plan and twice impersonating employees for an alcohol licence; the San Francisco shop fell from 94,000 to 64,000 dollars; the AI Village's cumulative output is 2,000 dollars of charity fundraising and 98 Substack subscribers

LEAP wave 8 (fielded 20 April to 11 May 2026) puts the superforecaster median AGI year at 2047 with only 80 per cent before 2100, and economists at 60 per cent before 2100. The most rigorously elicited large panel implies well under 30 per cent before 2035, and Polymarket prices only about 11 per cent on any AGI announcement before end-2027

Strict-definition distributions retain long right tails - the cross-platform aggregate is about 2031 with an 80 per cent interval running to 2044 (15 July 2026), and Metaculus's flagship median is January 2033 - implying roughly 26-32 per cent of mass falls after 2035

Physical and governance friction compounding - 30 to 50 per cent of 2026 data-centre capacity expected to slip, only about 5 of 12 announced GW actually under construction (Sightline Climate), interconnection queues of five years or more, PJM short 7 GW; EU AI Office enforcement live from August 2026 at the 10^25 FLOP threshold; and all three leading labs have publicly endorsed building coordinated-pause capacity

key_uncertainties: Whether any frontier lab ever applies the word AGI to a system it has shipped, now that the OpenAI-Microsoft clause that gave the term contractual force was removed on 27 April 2026 and the field has drifted to 'powerful AI', 'transformative AI' and graded taxonomies

Whether the messy-task gap evidenced by AA-Briefcase (about 3 per cent full-task completion), the Andon Labs shops and the AI Village is a scaffolding problem that agent architectures close within a generation or two, or a deep architectural limit on out-of-distribution generalisation and original insight that blocks recursive self-improvement entirely

How hard the post-2030 compute ceiling actually binds - whether chip and memory saturation genuinely halves the hazard rate in the 2030-2035 window, or whether algorithmic efficiency, new fab capacity or an architectural unlock keeps effective compute growing at 2026 rates

Whether the 'three or more leading AI researchers' limb is far easier than it looks - Huang, Altman, Goertzel and arguably Amodei have each made statements a lenient resolver could already count - and how strictly this tracker's resolver would police 'leading' and 'achieved'

How much weight to place on the LEAP superforecaster median of 2047 versus market-implied and lab-leader medians eight to twenty years earlier; the spread across serious anchors remains wider than my entire confidence interval

forecasts.key_change:
Hold at 7. The 22-23 August window produced no new information that bears on the mechanism, and what little arrived leans mildly disconfirming. I keep the central estimate at 7 percent and the interval at 4-11.

Start with the raw activity data, because that is where a genuine change would show first. Taiwan's MND reported at 6am on 23 August zero PLA aircraft, 7 PLAN vessels and 7 official ships, explicitly noting that no flight path illustration was provided because no PLA aircraft were detected in the period. On 22 August it reported 3 sorties, 8 PLAN and 7 official ships, with 3 of 3 sorties crossing the median line into the northern and southwestern ADIZ. On 21 August it again reported zero aircraft, with 7 PLAN and 6 official ships. On 20 August it was 7 sorties, 8 PLAN and 6 official ships. Two of the last three daily reports carry no PLA aircraft at all, and the three-day air total of three sorties is among the lowest readings of 2026 - against 14 sorties on 6 August and routine 2024-25 days in the twenty-to-forty range. This matters for a specific reason: yesterday I recorded a fall from 20 sorties to 3. Today it went to zero. That is not a lull inside a build-up; a build-up does not stand its air component down for two days in three. I should be careful not to over-read three days of noise in either direction, but the direction is unambiguously away from escalation.

Second, an absence that is itself evidence. The ISW-AEI China and Taiwan Update of 21 August, data cutoff 20 August, contains no PLA air or naval activity section, no median-line or joint-patrol reporting, no China Coast Guard activity around Kinmen or quarantine-style operations against Taiwan, and no PLA leadership or purge item. When the most systematic weekly tracker in the field runs a Taiwan edition with no Taiwan military-activity content, the base state is quiet.

No reservist call-up, no RO-RO requisition, no blood or medical stockpiling, no evacuation of nationals. Jamestown's Pratas count is 52 patrol voyages in 2024, 46 in 2025 and 19 in the first five months of 2026, which annualises flat to slightly down. Grey-zone pressure is chronic, not accelerating. The one item that deserves more weight than I have given it is the January 2026 "floating wall" - an L-shaped array of thousands of Fujian and Zhejiang militia fishing vessels stretching some 300 miles and disrupting Strait traffic for over 30 hours. forecasts.base_rate:
Four reference classes bear on this question, and I weight the first and fourth most heavily.

The broad class is major-power initiation of an opposed amphibious assault, or a sustained naval blockade of a defended and populated territory, since 1945. The candidate set is thin: Inchon in 1950 against a state already at war, Suez in 1956, the Cuban quarantine of 1962 which was a partial interdiction lasting under a month, the Falklands in 1982 which was a British counter-invasion of a lightly garrisoned archipelago, the Iran-Iraq tanker war of 1984-88, and Russia's Black Sea grain interdiction from 2022. Roughly six episodes across eighty years, against a denominator of perhaps twenty to thirty dyads at any time possessing both capability and a claimed casus belli. That implies an annualised hazard per capable dyad of roughly 0.5 to 2 percent. Applied to the 3.36 years from 23 August 2026 to 1 January 2030, that yields about 2 to 7 percent. The class is small, the cases are heterogeneous in scale, and the modern nuclear and economically interdependent context is poorly represented by the mid-century entries. Its value is as a discipline against salience.

The second class is Taiwan Strait coercion episodes specifically. Since 1995 there have been seven salient ones: the 1995-96 missile crisis, the August 2022 post-Pelosi encirclement, Joint Sword 2024A in May and 2024B in October, Strait Thunder in April 2025, Justice Mission 2025 in December, and the January 2026 militia floating wall. None produced a blockade exceeding 72 hours or an assault. The longest disruption on record is roughly 30 hours in January 2026; the August 2022 closure areas were announced, time-boxed and did not produce interdiction that news agencies characterised as a blockade. A naive Laplace estimate on zero-for-seven gives roughly 11 percent per episode, and at the observed rate of about one episode every eighteen months one would expect two more before 2030, implying something above 20 percent. I reject that arithmetic. It treats deliberately calibrated signalling exercises as independent draws on a war lottery, when in every case the PRC controlled the end date in advance and announced it. The correct inference from this class is about the ceiling of routine coercion - which is high and rising - not about the hazard of a decision for war. It is what makes the base state noisy, not what makes it dangerous.

The third class is deliberate irredentist initiation by a leader with a stated claim, capability and a domestic timeline: Argentina over the Falklands in 1982, Iraq over Kuwait in 1990, India over Goa in 1961, China over the Indian border in 1962, Russia over Crimea in 2014 and Ukraine in 2022. The class is not empty, strategic warning was short in most cases, and in several the initiator surprised analysts who had reasoned from cost. The common thread is that every initiator believed the operation would be short and cheap. That is the sharpest disanalogy here: the PLA's own literature treats a Taiwan landing as the hardest operation in modern warfare, and the quarantine option exists precisely because the assault option is not believed to be cheap. This class raises the floor and widens the upper tail; it does not set the central estimate.

The fourth consideration is the resolution bar and the shape of the hazard over the window. Decompose: the probability that Beijing initiates some materially escalated coercive action against Taiwan before 2030 - a declared quarantine, a customs-inspection regime, a closure area, an offshore-island seizure, a boarding of a Taiwan-bound merchant vessel - I would put at 20 to 30 percent, and the accreting legal and militia infrastructure documented through 2026 supports the upper half of that. But the conditional probability that such an action meets this question's terms, a blockade lasting more than 72 hours or an assault on Taiwan proper, confirmed by two or more major news agencies, is considerably lower - perhaps 25 to 35 percent. Beijing's revealed preference is for actions that are undeclared, sub-threshold, law-enforcement-framed and reversible, precisely because that forecloses third-party intervention. The product of those two ranges lands at roughly 5 to 10 percent.

Hazard is also not uniform across the window. It is depressed through late 2026 by the 21st Party Congress preparation, the September Washington state visit and November APEC in Shenzhen, and by a CMC reduced to Xi plus Zhang Shengmin after the January 2026 removals of Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli. It rises through 2027-2029 with the PLA centenary capability milestone, the January 2028 Taiwan presidential election, a rebuilt command layer and the projected trough in US munitions and hull availability. Roughly 15 percent of the window's probability mass sits in the remainder of 2026, with the balance concentrated in 2028-29.

Blending: the outside-view class centres near 4 percent, the deliberate-decision class argues for a fatter tail, and the decomposition centres near 7. External anchors - prediction markets and expert surveys have generally sat in the 5-12 percent band for a pre-2030 blockade or invasion - are consistent. I take 7 percent with an interval of 4 to 11.

forecasts.question: Will UK annual CPI inflation fall below 2.0% for at least one month before 1 January 2027?
forecasts.key_change:
Hold at 1%. The 80% interval stays at [0, 1]. Four days after the July 2026 CPI print, the incoming information is either neutral or points the wrong way for a YES, and the structural constraint that dominates this question has now been fully verified rather than inferred.

The latest published figure is the anchor. ONS published Consumer price inflation, UK: July 2026 on 19 August 2026, showing the CPI annual rate at 2.9%, up from 2.6% in June and the highest in four months. The monthly rate was +0.3%. CPIH was 3.1% and core CPI (excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco) was 2.6%, unchanged from June and above the 2.5% consensus. Services inflation was 3.4%, down from 3.6% in June. The largest contributing division was housing and household services at 0.59 percentage points of the headline rate, reflecting the 13% July increase in the Ofgem cap, with gas prices up 14.7% and electricity up 3.6% on the month. So the question asks whether a rate currently at 2.9% will print at or below 1.9% within a very small number of remaining opportunities.

The mechanics are now nailed down. Only prints PUBLISHED before 1 January 2027 count, and I verified today that the ONS release page for Consumer price inflation, UK: December 2026 carries a release date of 20 January 2027 7:00am and is flagged "This release is not yet published". The December 2026 reference month is therefore definitively outside the window. Going the other way, the ONS release for "Contributions to the 12-month rate of CPIH by import intensity: November 2026" is scheduled for 16 December 2026 at 9:30am; that companion release always accompanies the main CPI bulletin published at 7:00am the same day, which pins the November 2026 reference month inside the window. The four in-scope reference months are therefore August 2026 (published 16 September), September 2026 (21 October), October 2026 (18 November) and November 2026 (16 December). Exactly four attempts, no more.

The arithmetic is close to determinative. From the July 2026 CPI index level of 142.9, hitting a headline rate of 1.9% or below requires the index to fall cumulatively between roughly 0.26% and 0.63% depending on which base month is used. October 2026 is the least demanding comparison because the October 2025 index rose 0.4% on the month to 139.8, so an October 2026 print of 1.9% needs the index at about 142.5, a fall of roughly 0.27% from July. Outside 2008-09 and 2020, the UK has not delivered a cumulative three-to-four month fall of that size in the inflation-targeting era, and certainly not while the administered energy component is rising.

What is new since the last re-forecast is modestly negative. Brent closed at USD 94.39 on 21 August 2026, marginally higher than the USD 93.86 to 95.29 range noted previously and the highest since July, after US officials' suggestions of an imminent Tehran deal failed to materialise and rhetoric re-escalated on both sides. Iran maintains that Hormuz stays closed unless Washington meets its conditions; Trump says the US has "total control" of the waterway. Roughly 8 million barrels a day are estimated lost. There is one faint positive: on 21 August Iran's president indicated Tehran wants the war to end soon, and oil was little changed on the session rather than rising further. That is a hint, not a turn. UK NBP gas rose toward 157 pence per therm on 21 August, recouping the previous session's losses, with European storage at 62%, the lowest seasonal level in records back to 2009 and the dominant driver of NBP from September onward.

The Ofgem October cap remains the single most important in-window administered price and it is still pending. The assessment window closed on 18 August, so every input is fixed and only the calculation is outstanding; confirmation is due by 26 August 2026. Cornwall Insight's final forecast is around GBP 1,709 on the new typical-consumption basis (GBP 1,899 on the old basis), against the current GBP 1,663, with the analyst range GBP 1,701 to GBP 1,747. That is a rise of roughly 3% to 5% net of the legislated removal of 5% VAT on domestic electricity from 1 October. An energy component that rises in October, feeding the October and November reference months, is close to fatal to a sub-2.0% print in the two months where the base effects are most favourable.

The disinflationary strands are real but far too small. Food and non-alcoholic beverages inflation fell to 1.3% in the year to July, and Worldpanel like-for-like grocery inflation eased to 2.1% in the four weeks to 9 August, the lowest since October 2024 and a fifth consecutive month of easing, with 31.3% of grocery spending on promotion, the highest share this year. Services at 3.4% is decelerating from 4.4% in January. Both are helpful for 2027; neither can remove a full percentage point from the headline in four months against a rising energy impulse.

No published forecaster has any in-window month below 2.0%. The Bank of England's July 2026 Monetary Policy Report has CPI peaking at about 3.2% in 2026 Q4 with risks "tilted to the upside". The MPC held Bank Rate at 3.75% on 29 July by 6-3, with Greene, Mann and Pill preferring a hike to 4.00% on energy-driven persistence concerns; there is no August MPR or MPC meeting in the 2026 calendar, with the next decision on 17 September 2026. A Reuters poll of 13-18 August found 56 of 64 economists expect no change for the rest of the year. HM Treasury's independent average has Q4 2026 CPI at 3.4% to 3.7%. The BCC does not see 1.9% until Q4 2027, a full year beyond this question's window.

I hold at 1% rather than 0 because I never assign zero. The residual mass covers an abrupt Hormuz settlement collapsing Brent and NBP before the October reference month, an unannounced fiscal measure with immediate index effect, and a small tail of ONS reweighting or revision that retrospectively places a month below 2.0%. Each is remote; together they are worth about a point.
forecasts.base_rate:
The primary reference class is the historical frequency with which UK CPI annual inflation has printed below 2.0% within four months of a reading in the 2.7% to 3.1% band. Using ONS CPI back to 1989, months in that band number in the low hundreds; the share followed within four months by a sub-2.0% print is on the order of 5% to 8%. That is the raw outside view, and it is already low. It also materially flatters the YES case here, for three structural reasons.

First, the episodes that actually delivered a full percentage point of disinflation in four months were driven by sharp negative energy shocks, tax cuts, or demand collapses, not by gradual services cooling. The clearest cases are 2008-09, when the financial crisis coincided with a temporary VAT cut to 15%; 2014-15, when oil roughly halved and CPI fell from around 1.6% to zero over eight months; and 2020, when the pandemic combined with VAT reductions and Eat Out to Help Out to compress the index. In every case the impulse was of the opposite sign to what is happening now. Brent is at USD 94.39 as of 21 August 2026 and rising, NBP is near 157 pence per therm, European storage is at a record-low seasonal 62%, and the Ofgem cap is set to rise again from 1 October. Conditioning the reference class on "energy impulse rising" rather than "energy impulse falling" cuts the historical hit rate to something close to zero: I cannot identify a single UK episode in the inflation-targeting era where CPI fell from near 3% to below 2% within four months while regulated energy prices were increasing.

Second, the reference class ignores the publication constraint, which is the binding feature of this question. A conventional "will inflation fall below X by date Y" question gives roughly the number of months implied by the calendar. This one does not: because the December 2026 reference month publishes on 20 January 2027, verified today on the ONS release page, the question effectively closes with the November 2026 data on 16 December 2026. Four attempts. Each attempt is highly correlated with the others, because they share the same energy base, the same cap trajectory and the same services momentum. This is not four independent draws at a 5% to 8% hazard; it is closer to one correlated draw with a low probability, which is why naive multiplication of monthly hazards would badly overstate the answer.

Third, a useful second reference class is forecast-error-based. Take the distribution of Bank of England four-quarter-ahead CPI forecast errors, which over the past two decades has a standard deviation of roughly 1.0 to 1.3 percentage points, but with the mass of the large errors concentrated in shock years (2008, 2011, 2021-22) and almost entirely on the upside in recent history. The Bank's July 2026 MPR central path has CPI at about 3.2% in Q4 2026, with the MPC explicitly noting risks "tilted to the upside". Getting a monthly print below 2.0% inside the window requires an error of roughly 1.3 percentage points in the disinflationary direction over a horizon of two to four months, not four quarters. Over horizons that short, the standard deviation of CPI forecast errors is much smaller, on the order of 0.2 to 0.4 percentage points, because the energy, food and administered components are largely already observable. A 1.3 percentage point downside miss at a three-month horizon is a three-to-five sigma event on that distribution. That framing independently supports a probability in the low single digits or below, and is what stops me drifting the estimate upward on the strength of genuinely encouraging food and services data.

A third check comes from the cross-forecaster distribution. HM Treasury's panel of independent forecasters averaged 3.4% to 3.7% for Q4 2026 as of the June and July compilations. Deutsche Bank has been in the 3.3% to 3.5% range. The Bank has 3.2%. The BCC, the most optimistic identifiable UK forecaster, does not reach 1.9% until Q4 2027. The lowest point in any published UK inflation forecast for the four in-scope months is comfortably above 2.5%. When the entire published distribution sits more than half a percentage point above the threshold and the dispersion between forecasters is only a few tenths, the implied probability of the threshold being crossed is small even before adding the energy-direction adjustment.

Combining these: the raw band-based reference class gives 5% to 8%; conditioning on a rising rather than falling energy impulse cuts it by roughly an order of magnitude; the publication constraint removes two of the six calendar months a casual reading would assume; and the short-horizon forecast-error distribution puts the required miss at three or more sigma. The cross-forecaster distribution corroborates. That converges on 1%, which is where the estimate has been pinned and where it should stay absent a genuine regime change in energy prices.

forecasts.base_rate:
The naive reference class is "wide-release tentpole films that reach $1.5B worldwide". Fewer than fifteen titles in cinema history have managed it and the unconditional base rate for any given tentpole is low single digits. That was the correct frame in June 2026, before release. Applying it now would be a textbook base-rate error of exactly the kind superforecasting discipline exists to prevent: selecting a reference class that discards the single most informative piece of conditioning information available, namely that the event has already occurred and is published on both named resolution sources.

The governing reference class today is narrower and stranger: "published cumulative box office figures on a major aggregator that are subsequently restated below a milestone the film had already cleared, and stay restated". Framed that way the question is not about ticket sales at all. Nobody is forecasting future demand. The forecast is about the stability of an already-published, independently corroborated accounting figure over a 130-day horizon.

What is the historical rate of that? Essentially zero for revisions of this magnitude. Aggregators revise constantly, but revisions are overwhelmingly small, usually upward, and concentrated in the days after a weekend as estimates convert to actuals. Downward revisions do occur, and today's Box Office Mojo international restatement of $252.5M is a live example that usefully corrects any assumption these numbers are carved in stone. But note its character: it was a reconciliation between two competing international tallies, it moved the named sources into closer agreement rather than further apart, and it left the reported cume above $2B. I am aware of no modern case in which a major release's reported worldwide cume was restated downward by more than a quarter of its total and held there. The restatement required here is 27.2 per cent of the lower published figure, on both sources simultaneously, sustained for four months.

A second relevant reference class is "forecasting questions whose resolution condition is already satisfied and publicly reported months before the deadline". These resolve as expected at a rate indistinguishable from one. The residual failure modes are procedural rather than empirical: the question is voided or reworded, the resolver uses a source other than the two named, the resolver reads the wording idiosyncratically, or both sources become unavailable. The wording here is unusually forgiving. "Gross over $1.5B worldwide by 31 December 2026" is a cumulative-by-then test rather than a snapshot test, and it names two sources joined by "or", so either one satisfying the criterion suffices. Both currently do by wide margins, which means even total divergence between them cannot produce a NO so long as one stays above.

A third framing is worth stating explicitly. The film is still in wide release and still winning weekends four frames in. Its cume on 31 December will be materially higher than today's, plausibly by several hundred million once the international long tail and remaining major-market holdovers are counted. The buffer widens with time rather than narrowing. Every mechanical force acting on this number over the next four months pushes it away from the threshold.

Weighing these, the empirical base rate for an already-crossed, doubly-published, 37-per-cent-clear threshold reversing is far below 0.5 per cent. The dominant residual risk is resolver mechanics and question administration, not box office performance.
