forecasts.base_rate:
The governing reference class is not "will two firms grow into a threshold" but "a threshold is already exceeded on the public record by roughly 50% four months before the measurement date, in a domain with a monotonic underlying trend; will it still be exceeded then". That is a persistence question, and persistence questions with this structure resolve YES at very high rates. Across public forecasting platforms, questions whose resolution condition is already satisfied by a wide margin, with no identified mechanism for reversal, resolve YES in the high nineties. The correct anchor is 97-99%, and the residual is dominated by resolution mechanics rather than by the world changing.

Four narrower classes point the same way.

First, revenue trajectories of large private technology companies at $10bn-plus scale. Documented instances of a firm's disclosed annualised revenue falling more than 30% within two quarters, absent fraud or an exogenous demand collapse, are close to unrepresented. The available cases are Wirecard and FTX, where revenue was substantially fictitious, and the 2020 travel and hospitality shock, where the demand base physically disappeared. Neither template fits here: Anthropic's Q2 revenue is cash-collected and now carries an operating profit, and enterprise AI seat counts and API volumes are growing rather than vanishing. To fail, the combined figure would need to drop by roughly a third from $105bn, and that has essentially no precedent at this scale outside accounting fraud.

Second, the class of "leaked or reported private-company run rate later revised downward". This one is not empty. Run-rate figures reported by Bloomberg, The Information and the FT from investor decks and internal memos have historically been revised by 10-30% when audited financials appear, and the gross-versus-net principal-agent question under ASC 606 is exactly the kind of issue that produces such a revision. Base rate for a material downward restatement at IPO for a company with a contested revenue-recognition policy is perhaps 15-25%. But the relevant question is not whether a restatement happens; it is whether a restatement large enough to take $105bn below $70bn happens. That requires a 33% haircut on the combined figure, or roughly a 54% haircut on Anthropic alone. The largest number anyone credible has put on the table is OpenAI's $8bn allegation, about 12% of Anthropic's run rate. Even the aggressive commentary ceiling of 40% falls well short. Conditional on restatement, the probability it is large enough to flip the question is low, perhaps 5-10%, giving an unconditional contribution around 1-2pp.

Third, the class of "definitional ambiguity in a resolution criterion turns an apparently-cleared question into a dispute". This is the biggest single residual. Resolution says "the most recent credible reporting of each company's Q4 2026 ARR". Three conventions are live: exit-month annualised run rate (about $105bn today), a net-basis adjustment of Anthropic (about $97bn), and trailing-quarter recognised revenue annualised (about $73.2bn on Q2 data). Historically, questions relying on a metric that companies define inconsistently generate resolution disputes at rates in the 5-15% range. What pulls this down sharply here is that all three conventions currently clear, and projected forward to Q4 all three clear with substantial room, because Anthropic's sequential growth is so steep that even the most conservative convention roughly doubles by year end. The dispute risk therefore collapses into "does the resolver find a Q4-dated figure at all", which is close to assured given a public S-1 by end-August, an October listing, and quarterly investor updates from both firms.

Fourth, the class of "sector-wide financing shock disrupts a leading private firm's operations within four months". AI equities have already drawn down hard: the median of 49 AI and AI-infrastructure names sits about 40% below all-time highs, Nvidia shed $153bn of market capitalisation in a single session in the July rout, and the BIS and ECB have both warned publicly of a bust. But the transmission from equity drawdown to reported ARR is slow and indirect. Even in the 2000-2002 and 2008-2009 analogues, revenue at firms with contracted enterprise commitments fell over years, not months, and typically by 10-25% rather than 33%. Within a four-month window the probability that a financing shock cuts reported run rate by a third is well under 1%.

Aggregating: persistence anchor 98-99%, minus roughly 1-1.5pp for the combined restatement-plus-adversarial-convention branch, minus a few tenths for demand collapse and financing shock, minus a small allowance for the resolver failing to find Q4 figures and defaulting to something odd. That lands at 98.5-99. I take 99, with the interval floor at 98 to acknowledge the ASC 606 branch remains genuinely open until the public S-1 lands.

forecasts.question: Will UK average annual real GDP growth exceed 1.5% across the 2030s (2030-2039)?
forecasts.key_change:
Hold at 33. Nothing published on 22-23 August 2026 bears on a decade that starts in 2030. It is a weekend; there were no ONS, OBR or Bank of England releases. The only two items inside 72 hours with even indirect relevance are the S&P Global flash UK PMI of 21 August 2026, where the composite output index printed 52.5 against 52.2 in July and a 51.6 consensus, with flash services at 52.8 against 51.8 expected, and S&P's chief business economist pointing to roughly 0.3 per cent growth in Q3 helped by "sunny weather and tech investment"; and the ONS public sector finances bulletin for July 2026, published 21 August, showing financial-year-to-date borrowing of 56.7 billion pounds, 2.3 billion above the OBR's March path, with implied 10-year borrowing at about 5.05 per cent and 30-year at about 5.7 per cent in mid-August. Both are cyclical noise at a 14-year horizon. The PMI carries one detail that is not noise: private service-sector employment has now fallen for 23 consecutive months, the longest run since the survey began in 1996, which is consistent with the labour-input side of the 2030s arithmetic being weak rather than strong.

The substantive re-weighting today concerns the ONS Productivity flash estimate and overview of 18 August 2026, which I had underweighted. On the RTI-based measure the ONS itself now recommends as the best indicator, output per hour rose just 0.7 per cent in the year to Q2 2026, and the ONS states that absent the May-June Labour Force Survey collection failure its best estimate would have been 0.6 per cent. That is a sharp deceleration from 2.1 per cent in Q1 2026 and 3.1 per cent in Q3 2025, with a quarter-on-quarter fall of 0.8 per cent. The LFS-sourced measure is worse: output per hour down 0.2 per cent year on year and only 2.3 per cent above its 2019 average, which is roughly 0.3 per cent a year over seven years. Even the flattering RTI series is only 4.6 per cent above 2019, about 0.65 per cent a year. The ONS's own summary is that productivity growth "remains subdued compared with the stronger productivity trends seen before the 2008 global financial crisis". This is precisely the variable that has to carry the question, and the latest read on it is materially weaker than the 6pp of AI-diffusion optimism I carried yesterday deserves.

Against that, the industry decomposition in the same release keeps the AI channel alive rather than killing it. Information and communication made the largest single upward contribution to whole-economy output per hour growth relative to the 2019 average, at 2.8 percentage points, while human health and social work made the largest negative contribution at minus 0.9 points. So the ICT productivity signal is genuine but narrow, and the negative drag is coming from labour-intensive public-adjacent services. Whether that narrow signal broadens by the early 2030s remains the single biggest fork in this question, and one weak quarterly print does not resolve it.

The offsetting item, which I raised the forecast on yesterday and continue to hold, is the Blue Book 2026 article of 20 August 2026. Because resolution is on ONS-reported figures, the systematic direction of national accounts revisions is part of the resolution mechanism, not commentary. Cumulative 1997 to 2024 volume growth was revised from 59.2 to 61.7 per cent, the mean revision to annual volume growth across 1998 to 2024 was plus 0.06 percentage points, 2024 growth went up 0.1 points to 1.1 per cent, and the 2010-2019 decade average went up 0.1 points to 2.1 per cent. A persistent wedge of that size, if it survives into 2030s vintages, is worth several points of probability on a threshold question.

These two considerations roughly cancel, which is why I hold rather than trim. The medium-term anchors are unchanged and all sit at or below the bar: the IMF's 2026 Article IV, concluded by the Board on 16 July 2026, judges 2025 growth of 1.4 per cent to have been "at its potential rate" and expects growth to "stabilize around potential in the medium term" after slowing to 1.0 per cent in 2026 on the energy price shock; Bank of England staff put current potential supply growth at 0.3 to 0.4 per cent (April 2026 MPR); the OBR's March 2026 EFO has TFP growth rising only gradually to 0.8 per cent by 2030, and market commentary ahead of the 28 October 2026 Budget expects a further cut of 0.1 to 0.2 points. The OECD's latest UK chapter has 1.2 per cent in 2026 and 1.3 per cent in 2027 and flags "high and volatile energy prices, rising fiscal pressures, weak productivity growth". Near-term consensus has ticked up marginally, with the HM Treasury August comparison averaging 1.1 per cent for 2026 against 1.0 per cent in July, NIESR's Summer 2026 outlook upgraded to 1.1 per cent for both 2026 and 2027, but EY at 0.9 per cent and KPMG at 0.7 per cent.

On whether the two-week drift from 34 to 32-33 is evidence-driven rather than self-reinforcing: it is evidence-driven. It traces to the 18 August productivity flash, the sustained 5.7 per cent 30-year gilt, industrial electricity at 24 pence per kWh in 2026 (46 per cent above the IEA member median, 11.9 per cent annualised growth since 2021), the BCC Q2 2026 survey finding only 17 per cent of firms planning to raise investment, a post-pandemic low, and anticipation of an OBR productivity downgrade in October. But two genuinely positive items landed in the same window: Blue Book's upward revision bias, and business investment up 1.7 per cent quarter on quarter in the Q2 2026 provisional estimate, with ICT and other machinery outperforming. I am therefore stopping the drift here and will not move again absent the 30 September quarterly national accounts or the 28 October EFO.
forecasts.base_rate:
The reference class is UK decade averages of annual real GDP growth as the ONS reports them, using the post-Blue Book 2026 vintage published 20 August 2026.

Decade averages of annual real GDP growth: 1950s roughly 2.6 per cent; 1960s roughly 3.1 per cent; 1970s roughly 2.4 per cent; 1980s roughly 2.7 per cent; 1990s roughly 2.2 per cent; 2000s roughly 1.8 per cent, including the 4.5 per cent fall in 2009; 2010-2019 now 2.1 per cent on the revised vintage, up 0.1 points. That is seven completed decades, and all seven exceed 1.5 per cent. Taken naively that is a base rate of 7 out of 7, or 100 per cent, with N equal to 7. The 2020s so far are the outlier: 2020 minus 10.3 per cent, 2021 plus 8.6 per cent, 2022 plus 4.8 per cent, 2023 about plus 0.5 per cent revised, 2024 plus 1.1 per cent revised, 2025 about plus 1.4 per cent, giving a six-year mean of roughly 0.8 per cent, and roughly 1.0 per cent across 2023-2025 alone.

That naive base rate is close to worthless and I do not use it as my anchor. Seven decade averages from one country are not seven independent draws; they are a single, heavily serially correlated time series, and the standard error on any inference is enormous. Worse, the sample is drawn overwhelmingly from a regime that no longer exists: rising working-age population, catch-up productivity, expanding female participation, financial deepening, and EU market integration. Every one of those has either exhausted itself or reversed.

The disciplined approach is to decompose. Decade real GDP growth equals growth in labour input plus growth in output per hour. On the labour side, the ONS 2024-based national population projections have the working-age population rising from 44.3 million to 45.8 million between mid-2024 and mid-2034, about 0.33 per cent a year, with natural change turning negative from mid-2026 as deaths exceed births, net migration falling to 138,000 in 2026 before the projection assumes stabilisation near 230,000, and the pensionable-age population up 1.8 million or 14.6 per cent over the same decade. Hours per worker have trended down. Realistically labour input contributes somewhere between 0.2 and 0.5 percentage points a year through the 2030s, against roughly 1.0 to 1.1 points in the 2010s when employment growth did most of the work.

That means productivity has to deliver roughly 1.0 to 1.3 percentage points a year for a decade to clear the bar. What has it actually delivered? Output per hour grew about 0.5 per cent a year across 2010-2019. Since 2019 it is 4.6 per cent higher on the RTI basis, about 0.65 per cent a year, or 2.3 per cent higher on the LFS basis, about 0.3 per cent a year (ONS, 18 August 2026). Year on year in Q2 2026 it was plus 0.7 per cent on RTI, minus 0.2 per cent on LFS. Pre-crisis, 1997-2007, it ran near 2 per cent. So YES requires productivity growth roughly double to triple the realised post-2008 rate, sustained for ten years.

Official potential estimates bracket the threshold from below. Bank of England staff put current potential supply growth at 0.3 to 0.4 per cent a year (April 2026 MPR). The OBR's March 2026 EFO has TFP growth gradually reaching 0.8 per cent by 2030, which implies whole-economy potential growth of roughly 1.4 to 1.5 per cent once labour and capital deepening are added, that is, sitting exactly on the bar, and the OBR has a long documented record of revising productivity down rather than up since 2010. The IMF's 2026 Article IV puts potential at about 1.4 per cent. NIESR's trend estimate is about 1.25 per cent.

Putting this together: my central estimate of the 2030-2039 decade mean is roughly 1.2 to 1.3 per cent, with a standard deviation around 0.5 percentage points reflecting genuine uncertainty over AI diffusion, migration policy, recession timing and measurement. Under a normal approximation, P(mean above 1.5 per cent) lands at roughly 27 to 34 per cent. Two adjustments push toward the upper end. First, ONS revision bias: a persistent plus 0.05 to 0.1 percentage point a year wedge in reported versus first-vintage growth, evidenced by Blue Book 2026's mean plus 0.06 point revision across 1998-2024, directly raises the reported number this question resolves on. Second, output-gap arithmetic: with unemployment near 5 per cent and payrolled employment falling, a downturn before 2030 is plausible, and recovery growth landing inside 2030-2039 would flatter the decade mean by perhaps 0.4 to 0.6 points, exactly as reflation from the 6.3 per cent peak-to-trough fall flattered the 2010s. That is why 33 rather than 27.

The historical 7-out-of-7 record deserves some weight as a caution against over-extrapolating stagnation, but the mechanism decomposition dominates it. Anchor: 33.

factors_up.factor: Blue Book 2026 (ONS, 20 August 2026) confirms persistent upward revision bias in ONS-reported real growth, which is the exact metric this question resolves on: mean revision +0.06pp a year across 1998-2024, cumulative 1997-2024 volume growth revised from 59.2% to 61.7%, 2024 growth up 0.1pp to 1.1%, 2010-2019 decade average up 0.1pp to 2.1%

AI/ICT productivity signal is visible and large where it exists: ONS productivity release of 18 August 2026 shows information and communication contributing +2.8pp to whole-economy output per hour growth relative to the 2019 average, the largest single upward industry contribution, and S&P Global's 21 August flash PMI attributes part of August's 52.5 composite reading to tech investment

Output-gap mechanics: with service-sector employment falling for 23 straight months (S&P Global, 21 August 2026) and unemployment near 5%, a downturn before 2030 is plausible; recovery growth landing inside 2030-2039 would mechanically lift the decade mean by roughly 0.4-0.6pp, as reflation flattered the 2010s to 2.1%

Historical decade base rate: seven completed decades from the 1950s to the 2010s all exceeded 1.5% (2.6, 3.1, 2.4, 2.7, 2.2, 1.8, 2.1), so a sub-1.5% decade would be unprecedented in the modern UK record even though the mechanisms that produced those decades have weakened

Supply-side runway before 2030: business investment up 1.7% q/q in the Q2 2026 provisional estimate with ICT and other machinery outperforming, a UK infrastructure pipeline now above 700bn pounds over ten years (up around 200bn since July 2025), an updated NPPF due in force summer 2026, and the British Industrial Competitiveness Scheme cutting electricity costs from 2027

factors_down.factor: Latest productivity data is materially weaker than the trend the question needs: ONS 18 August 2026 flash shows RTI output per hour up only 0.7% y/y in Q2 2026 (0.6% adjusting for the LFS collection failure), down from 2.1% in Q1 and 3.1% in Q3 2025, with a -0.8% q/q fall; the LFS measure was -0.2% y/y and just 2.3% above its 2019 average, about 0.3% a year

Demographics leave productivity doing almost all the work: ONS 2024-based projections have working-age population rising from 44.3m to 45.8m over mid-2024 to mid-2034, about 0.33% a year, with deaths exceeding births from mid-2026, net migration falling to 138,000 in 2026, and the pensionable-age population up 14.6% over the decade

Every official potential-growth anchor sits at or below the bar: Bank of England staff potential supply growth 0.3-0.4% (April 2026 MPR), OBR TFP growth reaching only 0.8% by 2030 (March 2026 EFO) with analysts expecting a further 0.1-0.2pp cut at the 28 October 2026 Budget, IMF potential about 1.4% with 2025 growth of 1.4% judged to be at potential (2026 Article IV, 16 July 2026), NIESR trend about 1.25%

Energy costs as a structural drag: UK industrial electricity at 24 pence per kWh in 2026, 46% above the IEA member median and up 11.9% annualised since 2021, with supported industry paying 86 pounds per MWh against 69 in France and 60 in Germany; the IMF attributes the 2026 slowdown to 1.0% directly to an energy price shock

Fiscal and investment-intent drag: July 2026 public sector finances (21 August) show 56.7bn pounds borrowed financial-year-to-date, 2.3bn above the OBR path, with 30-year gilts near 5.7% and 10-year at 5.05%, a third successive tax-raising Budget due 28 October 2026, and the BCC Q2 2026 survey finding only 17% of firms plan to raise investment, a post-pandemic low

key_uncertainties: Whether AI diffusion broadens from the narrow ICT and professional services slice (6-8% of GVA, but contributing +2.8pp to whole-economy output per hour growth since 2019) into health, construction, retail and public services by the early 2030s. Published UK estimates span from negligible to double-digit percentage GDP gains by 2030, a range wide enough to be nearly uninformative

Whether the ONS measurement wedge persists: if the +0.05 to +0.1pp a year upward revision bias evidenced in Blue Book 2026 carries into 2030s vintages, it materially changes the odds of a reported decade mean clearing 1.5%; if the new component-based labour productivity methodology (methods article due September 2026) or the LFS-RTI reconciliation moves things the other way, the wedge could reverse

Whether the UK has a recession before 2030 rather than inside the window. A downturn in the late 2020s followed by recovery growth inside 2030-2039 lifts the decade mean by perhaps 0.4-0.6pp; a recession inside the window cuts it by a similar amount. This alone makes the distribution wide and mildly bimodal

Whether net migration settles near the ONS long-run assumption of about 230,000 a year or stays nearer the 138,000 projected for 2026. The gap is worth roughly 0.2-0.3pp a year on headline GDP growth through the 2030s, which is a large fraction of the distance to the threshold

Whether the OBR's 0.8% medium-term TFP assumption is too optimistic or too pessimistic. It has been revised down repeatedly since 2010 and another cut is widely expected on 28 October 2026, but the November 2025 cut may already have overshot, and OBR's own AI-adoption alternative scenario is materially more optimistic
update_triggers: Revise UP if the quarterly national accounts on 30 September 2026 and the follow-up Blue Book revisions article on 30 October 2026 show a further material upward revision to real growth in recent years, confirming the ONS reporting wedge is durable rather than a one-off

Revise UP if the ONS productivity flash for Q3 2026 on 17 November 2026 shows RTI-based output per hour growth back above 1.5% year on year, or if the new component-based methodology (methods article due September 2026) raises the measured level or trend of UK labour productivity

Revise UP if the OBR raises its medium-term trend productivity assumption at the 28 October 2026 Budget EFO, or if the Bank of England lifts its potential supply estimate above 0.3-0.4% in the November 2026 Monetary Policy Report

Revise UP if ONS industry-level output-per-hour decomposition shows AI-attributable gains spreading materially beyond information and communication into health and social work (currently -0.9pp), construction, retail or public services
Revise DOWN if the OBR cuts its trend productivity assumption again on 28 October 2026 by the 0.1-0.2pp analysts expect, or if the Budget package is scored as net contractionary for potential output

Revise DOWN if net migration settles durably below 150,000 a year, if working-age population growth to 2034 is revised below 0.3% a year, or if 30-year gilt yields sustain above 6% and force further cuts to public capital spending through the late 2020s
